Thank you very much, everyone. And good afternoon from Kabul. I just came back from Jalalabad, so I'm speaking to you from Kabul. The severe acute malnutrition cases which were admitted with medical complications have actually risen by more than a third this year. For example, in July 2025, we recorded around 6,000 cases, but for this year, our numbers are already eating and going beyond 8,000 cases. In parts of southern Afghanistan, some hospitals are now seeing three of four severe malnourished children for every available bed. I have just returned, like you said, from Nangarhar, and I was at the Nangarhar Regional Hospital in Eastern Afghanistan, where I went into the nutrition ward, and I met a young mother with a nine-month-old daughter, and the daughter's name is Sajida. Sajida came. from a remote province not far from Nangarhar, the province of Nuristan. And this is a province that recently was affected by severe flash flood. And during that crisis, a UNICEF trained female community health worker found Sajida there suffering from severe acute malnutrition and referred her to the regional hospital. When Sajida first got on admission in the hospital, The doctors had little hope that she was going to survive. She weighed barely four kilograms, but after receiving therapeutic milk and other nutrition services and support, she's now stable. When I met her two days ago in Nangarhar, she was still very frail. My hope is that Sajida will survive, although I acknowledge that she has not completely come out of the woods. And Sajida is just one of the many children suffering from malnutrition in Afghanistan. But it's not only in the east. What I witnessed in the southern part of the country when I visited the regional hospital in Kandahar in July, which provides services to five provinces in the southern region of the country, is similar. I saw many young children with complications from malnutrition being treated. These cases reflect a much bigger and increasingly alarm picture across the country. But today, I also want to draw attention to something that happened before a child reaches the stage of being in a hospital bed. Last month, for example, UNICEF released a new report that we titled, Too Little Too Late, the Diet Crisis Facing Young Children in Afghanistan. And in that report, for the very first time, in the scale that we did the analysis, UNICEF was able to analyze child malnutrition across Afghanistan, bringing focus to actually what our children are eating in the homes. And the findings are very concerning. Families begin cutting back on nutritious food. Children are eating fewer different types of food. Meals are becoming smaller and sometimes meals are skipped. And in some instances, children do go hungry. Half of Afghanistan children are living in what we call severe child food poverty. And what this means is that they are eating food from just two or fewer food groups that they require to grow and develop. And when children reach the age of six months, and when they should start receiving nutritious complementary food alongside breast milk, the reality for many children and family is completely different. What we see is that a child's first food may consist of little more than bread with tea or some form of watered down yogurt. And for a growing child, this is simply not enough. The UNICEF analysis also shows that children living in severely food insecure household can have up to six times more likelihood to suffer from wasting during the peak malnutrition period in the country. Wasting is one of the most dangerous form of malnutrition that a child can be exposed to. If I put it in a simple way, this means that the children are becoming dangerously thin for their height, and often because they are getting not enough nutritious food, but also because they are sick or a combination of both. Without timely care, it can become life-threatening, and we are seeing many of that in our hospital beds. But malnutrition in Afghanistan is not only about the lack of food. A child who is already poorly nourished and then develops severe diarrhea or respiratory infection can deteriorate very quickly. And a child who repeatedly becomes sick in turns with much more continually become malnourished. So it becomes a vicious cycle for those children that are experiencing these on the ground. This year alone, this longstanding problem have been compounded by several additional pressures that we are experiencing in Afghanistan. For example, Afghanistan has endured successful years of drought, floods, destructive rain, and also many flash floods like I mentioned in Northeast. And with this year's super El Nino coming, the impact of climate related shocks are projected to be more intense and will have more implication for children and by extension, malnutrition. At the same time, regional instability is disrupting cross-border trade and livelihood. Six million people more than half of whom are children who have already returned to Afghanistan since 2023, are putting additional pressures on jobs and on livelihood. And they are also putting additional pressures on essential health and nutrition services, which in themselves are already stretched to the limit. In Nangarhar, for example, I met with these returnees in the last few days. And I met families who have returned whose children are receiving care and treatment for malnutrition at the regional hospital. All of this is happening in a context where families have limited opportunities for livelihood. In southern Afghanistan, some hospitals are currently seeing three or four severely malnourished children for every available bed. And even when we successfully treat a child, the story is not over because treatment alone is not enough. Yes, treatment saves life, but that is not enough. When a surviving child is sent back home into households that still cannot afford nutritious food or would you not have access to clean drinking water or a household that cannot access basic healthcare services. We frequently see those kind of children relapse and come back for further treatment. And this is why the new evidence from UNICEF matters in the sense that it allows us to shift focus a lot more to prevention. It gives us an opportunity to identify the warning signs early enough and to act before a child reaches the point of severe malnutrition. We need to protect the nutrition of women during pregnancy as well. We need to support breastfeeding. And when a baby reaches six months of age, we need to help the family to provide the diversity and nutritious food that a child needs to grow. We also need to ensure access to healthcare services, sanitation and hygiene is in place, in addition to immunization services and social protection services, because all of these needs to work hand in hand around the same vulnerable family. UNICEF and our partners are working to do exactly this, including through our first food initiatives with a particular focus on children between the age of six and 23 months. But this is actually where we face a contradiction, a contradiction in the sense that at precisely the moment when the needs are increasing, the services available to children are being reduced due to funding cuts. More than 100 sites that treat children with severe wasting have closed when we compare to what we had in 2025, mainly because of resource constraint. 100 most centers that provide nutrition support to children and malnourished pregnant and breastfeeding women have also lost funding. And today, the nutrition sector response in Afghanistan faces around a 57% funding shortfall. Specifically for UNICEF, the situation is even more stark. Our nutrition program in Afghanistan that is estimated at 180 million this year is currently only 22% funded. And this is happening while the number of children that need our help is increasing. So the message I want to leave with you today is very simple. We can see that this crisis is coming. We can see it in what our children are eating in Afghanistan. We can see it in the increasing number of very young children who are becoming malnourished. We can see it in the overcrowded hospital wards where three to four sick children are admitted on available beds. And we can also see it in the child like Sajida whom I met few days ago in Nangarhar. But seeing a crisis coming also means that we have an opportunity to prevent it from becoming much worse. We should not wait until a child is dangerously thin and lying in a hospital bed before we act. For that, UNICEF and our partners, we are urgently reaching out for flexible and sustainable funding to scale up prevention, but also treatment services in the country. Because when it comes to malnutrition, acting early does not only save lives, it also ensure far more cost effective intervention because we are able to avert major crises that have lifelong implication. We know what is happening. We know that many children are at risk. We also know what to do to prevent and treat malnutrition to avoid a major crisis ahead of us. I am therefore reaching out to the international community to come round and support UNICEF and partners so that we can provide the required services and support to the children of Afghanistan. I thank you very much for the opportunity. Back to you.
